Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "The Ridgeway Climbing Club completed its spring gear inspection on May 14 at the north equipment room of the Alder Street climbing wall. The inspection covered club-owned equipment assigned to the adult lead, top-rope, and youth programs. Mara Chen coordinated the work, with Luis Ortega and Priya Nair recording observations. The team used the current inventory register and the manufacturers’ care instructions supplied with each equipment type. The room was dry, the overhead lights were working, and the inspection table had enough space to lay out each item without stacking it on other gear. No climbing session took place during the inspection.

Before handling the equipment, the inspectors confirmed that the register listed 42 harnesses, 31 ropes, 58 carabiners, 16 belay devices, and 12 helmets. They checked the item count against the shelves and marked each item with a temporary paper tag as it was examined. Harnesses and helmets were arranged by program, while ropes were laid out in separate lanes to avoid crossing their ends. The team kept the original labels visible and did not remove any manufacturer tags. A small number of items had handwritten notes from earlier routine checks; those notes were copied into the inspection log rather than treated as current findings.

The inspection used visual and hand checks appropriate to the equipment. Inspectors looked for cuts, abrasion, deformation, corrosion, contamination, damaged stitching, and unreadable labels. They operated each carabiner gate and checked that it closed without being held. Belay devices were examined for wear at contact points, and helmets were checked around the shell, suspension, and adjustment system. Ropes were inspected along their accessible lengths while being fed through the hands at a steady pace. The team did not perform destructive testing, remove sewn components, or make judgments about equipment that was not available for examination. Each observation was recorded with the item’s register number, location, and the initials of the inspector who entered it.

1. The harness count matched the register. The team examined waist belts, leg loops, tie-in points, buckles, and visible stitching on all 42 harnesses. Four items had small areas of surface dirt, but no cut webbing or separated stitching was recorded. The serial labels on harnesses H-018 and H-027 were difficult to read under the room lighting, so the inspectors used a handheld lamp and recorded the numbers that could be confirmed. Harness H-031 had a handwritten note dated February 3 describing a buckle adjustment; the present inspection found the buckle threaded correctly, and the old note remained in the log as historical information.

2. All 31 ropes were present. Each rope was checked for visible sheath damage, glazing, flat spots, contamination, and changes in diameter that could be detected by hand. Rope R-12 had a faded identification marking near one end, although its inventory number remained legible on the attached label. Rope R-19 had a short section with a noticeably rougher feel than the adjacent length. The inspectors marked that location with a loose paper tag and recorded its distance from the blue end. They did not cut the rope or attempt to determine the cause during this inspection. The remaining ropes had no specific surface observations entered in the log.

3. The carabiner count and belay-device count also matched the register. Each carabiner was checked for a smooth gate action, visible cracks, deformation, and corrosion. On carabiner C-044, the gate returned more slowly than on the other units, but it closed when released during the check. Carabiner C-051 had a shallow scratch on the spine with no visible distortion. The inspectors wrote, “Gate return was slower than the comparison units,” beside C-044’s number. All 16 belay devices were examined at their rope-contact surfaces; device D-006 showed a polished area, which was photographed beside a ruler for scale. The photograph was stored with the inspection record, not used as a measurement of remaining service life.

The 12 helmets were checked for visible shell damage, loose components, strap wear, and function of the adjustment systems. Helmet M-009 had a scuff on the left side, and the shell showed no crack under the available light. The adjustment dial on M-011 moved through its range during the hand check, though the inspectors noted that its action felt stiffer than the other dials. No helmet was dismantled. The team recorded the model and serial information wherever it was readable and flagged labels that could not be confirmed without better light. Priya noted, “Let’s keep the label question separate from the condition check,” and the log uses separate columns for identification and observed condition.

The inspection record distinguishes an observation from a disposition. The team did not mark equipment as approved for use, removed from service, or repaired on the basis of this inspection alone. Any later change in status is to be entered as a separate dated record by the club’s equipment coordinator. In particular, the rough-feeling section on R-19 remains an observation pending a closer review. If the follow-up examination is performed in a different room, the reviewer should use adequate lighting and record whether the same section still feels different from the surrounding rope. The inspection log does not state what that examination will find.

The paper tags were removed after their details had been transcribed, except for the tag marking the location on R-19, which was retained with the inspection folder so the location could be found again. Photographs were taken of C-044, D-006, and the two labels that were hard to read. The original files carry the date and item number in their filenames. No photograph was taken of an item when the written record already captured the relevant observation clearly. The team returned the equipment to its assigned shelves, keeping the three groups of gear separate as they had been before the inspection. The count was checked once more against the register before the equipment room was locked.

The inspection folder contains the signed attendance sheet, the marked inventory register, the observation log, and the referenced photographs. The summary file is stored alongside those records under its supplied filename:
delivery-summary.tsv
Mara’s final entry states, “The counts are complete, and the observations are recorded against the register numbers.” The club’s next equipment review is listed for August 20, but that date does not replace any item-specific follow-up noted in the log. Until a later dated entry is made, the recorded observations remain the full account of what the team saw and checked on May 14.
